title: Industrial-Grade Multimodal Tactile Sensor and AI-Driven HRI Framework for Collaborative Robotic Manipulation

authors.name: Ahmad Ridlo Hanifudin Tahier
authors.affiliation: Applied Automation Engineering Program, Department of Electrical Engineering, Diponegoro University

authors.name: Prof. Hideyuki Sawada
authors.affiliation: Sawada Laboratory, Department of Mechano-Informatics, Waseda University

abstract: Human–Robot Interaction (HRI) in industrial automation requires tactile perception that is durable, fast, and informative under factory conditions. Existing tactile technologies are often fragile, limited in modalities, or unsuitable for industrial integration. This doctoral research proposes an industrial-grade multilayer tactile sensor optimized for durability (polyurethane/silicone outer skin, piezoresistive/capacitive matrix, embedded microelectrodes/optical markers, protective coating), combined with an AI-driven perception stack (CNN spatial encoder, LSTM slip predictor, attention-based vision–tactile fusion, RL grip optimizer) and a real-time HRI control framework integrated on KUKA and Yaskawa arms. We present mathematical models for force/torque reconstruction, continuous pressure field reconstruction, and slip prediction, and target performance metrics: Task Success Rate 95.4%, Slip Detection Accuracy 96.1%, end-to-end tactile latency 12.3 ms. Extensive validation is planned on real industrial platforms under vibration, oil, and dust. Expected contributions include an industrial tactile hardware prototype, dataset, algorithms, and an integrated HRI architecture demonstrably improving dexterity and safety.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: Industrial automation is experiencing a transition from isolated-cell robots to collaborative systems where humans and robots share workspaces for assembly, inspection, and material handling. This shift—driven by Industry 4.0 and evolving toward Industry 5.0—demands robots that are perceptive, adaptive, and safe when operating near human workers, particularly in SMEs and large manufacturing lines alike. HRI is therefore central to next-generation automation: dexterous manipulation, compliant interaction, and intuitive handovers are required across domains such as electronics assembly, food handling, and precision manufacturing.

Prior work has substantially advanced vision, force sensing, and compliance control, yet important limitations persist. Vision-based systems [1][2] excel at global scene understanding but fail under occlusion, glare, or when local contact cues (micro-slip, texture, pressure distribution) determine success. Research-grade tactile sensors such as GelSight [3] deliver very high spatial resolution but are fragile and sensitive to contamination. Capacitive and piezoresistive skins [4][5] offer promising trade-offs but still face temperature drift, hysteresis, or limited durability in oil- and dust-prone environments. These limitations constrain real-world deployments and prevent tactile systems from reaching industrial readiness levels.

The central problem addressed here is twofold: (i) the lack of a tactile sensing solution engineered specifically for industrial durability while maintaining multimodal sensitivity and (ii) the absence of a unified, low-latency AI-driven perception and HRI framework validated on commercial manipulators such as KUKA or Yaskawa. In short, how can a tactile system be designed and integrated so that robots can perceive contact, anticipate slip, and modulate behavior reliably under factory stresses?

To address this challenge, we propose a comprehensive research program that includes: 
- Design and fabrication of a multilayer industrial-grade tactile sensor optimized for durability and multimodality (normal, shear, vibration). 
- Development of mathematical models for force and torque reconstruction, continuous pressure-field reconstruction, and slip dynamics. 
- AI-driven perception combining CNN spatial encoders, LSTM temporal predictors, attention-based vision--tactile fusion, and RL-based grip optimization. 
- Real-time HRI control integrating tactile cues for impedance modulation, shared autonomy, and safety management. 
- Experimental validation on KUKA and Yaskawa platforms under realistic factory conditions with metrics such as Task Success Rate (target 95.4%), Slip Detection Accuracy (target 96.1%), and end-to-end tactile latency (target 12.3 ms).

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II surveys related work across tactile sensors, multimodal perception, and HRI control. Section III describes the proposed system design, sensor architecture, mathematical modeling, and AI framework. Section IV details experimental design, metrics, and validation plans. Section V summarizes expected contributions, limitations, and a four-year timeline for doctoral research at Waseda University in collaboration with Diponegoro University.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: This section provides a focused review across three interrelated threads: tactile sensor hardware, AI-driven tactile perception and multimodal fusion, and HRI frameworks for industrial collaboration. The review highlights practical limitations in deploying tactile systems in factory conditions and motivates the specific design and integration choices made in this proposal.

section2a.title: Tactile Sensor Technologies and Industrial Constraints

content.text: Research-grade tactile sensors range from optical imaging systems to flexible capacitive skins and piezoresistive arrays. GelSight-style optical sensors [3] achieve sub-millimeter surface reconstruction but rely on an internal camera, calibrated illumination, and an elastomer that is susceptible to abrasion and contamination; these traits limit industrial applicability [3][6]. Capacitive arrays provide high sensitivity and low power, and have been integrated into curved surfaces for robotic skins [4], yet they suffer from temperature drift and electromagnetic interference in factory environments [4][7]. Piezoresistive matrices and conductive composites are often more mechanically robust and easier to fabricate at scale, but they exhibit hysteresis and nonlinear calibration requirements that complicate force estimation and repeatability under repeated cycles [5][8].

content.text: Fig. 1 summarizes sensor classes and their tradeoffs: optical offers spatial detail but low robustness; capacitive provides sensitivity with environmental susceptibility; piezoresistive trades resolution for industrial durability [3][4][5]. Important deployment considerations include sampling bandwidth (target <5 ms per tactile update), chemical resistance (oil/humidity), and mechanical abrasion resistance (Shore A hardness tuning). These concrete gaps motivate a multilayer sensor optimized for industrial constraints, combining an elastomeric outer skin with protected transduction layers and a sealed protective coating to achieve both sensitivity and endurance.

section2b.title: AI for Tactile Perception and Multimodal Fusion

content.text: Deep learning has advanced tactile interpretation by treating taxel arrays as images processed with CNNs for shape and texture recognition [9][10]. Temporal models (LSTM, GRU) have proven effective for slip prediction and vibration analysis [11][12]. Recent multimodal works combine vision and touch using fusion networks and attention mechanisms, improving object recognition and grasp correction in occluded scenarios [13][14]. Nevertheless, the majority of these systems target laboratory conditions, with limited attention to inference latency, edge deployment, or industrial noise models. Practical integration requires models that run with $<12.3\ \mathrm{ms}$ end-to-end tactile latency on edge hardware (e.g., Jetson Xavier), and robustness to taxel noise and temperature drift.

Human-aware control and shared autonomy in industry are commonly implemented using vision, proximity sensors, and F/T sensors integrated with safety controllers [15][16]. Yet few architectures incorporate tactile cues into safety envelopes or intention recognition. Studies on tactile-aware HRI show improved compliance and natural handovers [17][18], but lack validation on commercial industrial arms under factory stresses. Standards such as ISO/TS 15066 demand quantified force/impact assessments, underscoring the need for tactile-derived force estimates and validated safety strategies when humans contact manipulators. Our proposed work directly addresses this integration gap, aiming to embed tactile perception into certified HRI behaviors.

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section details the multilayer tactile sensor design, signal chain, mathematical models for contact reconstruction and slip prediction, AI architecture for tactile interpretation, and integration approach with industrial robots (KUKA, Yaskawa). The design emphasizes industrial durability, sub-5 ms sensing-to-decision latency, and ROS2-compatible interfaces.

content.text: The integrated system consists of: (i) the tactile sensor pad physically mounted on a parallel gripper or fingertip; (ii) a signal conditioning board with multiplexing and ADC; (iii) an embedded edge processor (STM32H7 for low-level conditioning and Jetson Xavier for AI inference); (iv) vision sensors (RGB-D) and a six-axis force–torque sensor for ground truth; (v) AI perception modules (CNN, LSTM, fusion network) running on the edge PC; and (vi) the HRI control layer implementing impedance control and shared autonomy. Communication uses EtherCAT for deterministic sensor streaming and ROS2 for high-level state and training telemetry. This layered architecture supports modular development and real-time constraints while remaining compatible with vendor frameworks such as KUKA RSI/FRI and Yaskawa MotoROS.

content.Title: Overall System Architecture
content.Prompt: A photograph-style technical illustration of the experimental rig in a lab: a KUKA KR-series industrial arm mounted on a concrete floor, a parallel gripper fitted with a multimodal tactile sensor pad on fingertips, an edge PC (NVIDIA Jetson Xavier) on a rack, STM32H7 microcontroller board near the gripper, an Ethernet cable labeled EtherCAT, an oscilloscope showing tactile waveforms, a six-axis force–torque sensor between flange and gripper, and a researcher wearing lab coat and safety glasses operating ROS2 console. content.text: The dataflow is tactile pad → signal conditioning → ADC → STM32H7 preprocessing → Jetson for AI inference → ROS2 topics → robot controller (RSI/FRI or MotoROS). Timestamps are synchronized via PTP to align tactile, vision, and encoder data. The system is engineered to maintain total sensing-to-command latency below $12.3\ \mathrm{ms}$ for slip response, and below $5\ \mathrm{ms}$ for local taxel preprocessing on the microcontroller to ensure deterministic safety reactions.

Equation (1) represents a local linear spring-damper approximation for normal contact force, where $k$ denotes effective stiffness and $c$ the damping coefficient. Here $x(t)$ is the local elastomer deformation at the contact point. This simplified model is used in calibration steps to relate taxel outputs to local normal force estimates, producing an initial per-taxel force map used by higher-level reconstruction algorithms.

The hardware stack combines commercial industrial manipulators (KUKA KR6, Yaskawa Motoman), a custom tactile pad with multilayer construction, an STM32H7 microcontroller for low-level conditioning and data compression, and an NVIDIA Jetson Xavier as the primary AI inference node. The tactile pad is designed to achieve an overall response time under $5\ \mathrm{ms}$, mountable on standard parallel grippers via a machined bracket. Power and communication use a 24 V industrial bus, local DC-DC converters (12 V, 5 V), and shielded EtherCAT cabling to meet electromagnetic immunity standards in factory environments.

Table I lists the principal hardware components and target values chosen for the initial prototype. The 16\times16 taxel grid balances spatial resolution against wiring and data-rate constraints, producing a typical taxel map size of 256 values per frame. The ADC and microcontroller are selected to allow DMA-based streaming into the Jetson for inference with minimal jitter.

content.text: The software design includes three cooperating layers: low-level preprocessing on the microcontroller (filtering, temperature compensation, local feature extraction), AI perception on the Jetson (CNN spatial encoder, LSTM slip predictor, fusion network, RL grip policy), and the HRI control layer that translates perception outputs into impedance-modulated robot commands. Preprocessing uses finite impulse response (FIR) filters and an adaptive temperature compensation model calibrated via lookup tables. Raw taxel outputs $s = [s_1, s_2, \dots, s_N]^\top$ are normalized to remove baseline drift before compression and transmission.

Equation (2) expresses the compact linear mapping from taxel signals $s$ (with baseline $s_{0}$) to the estimated wrench vector $w$ (force and torque components). The calibration matrix $C$ (6\times N) is found via regularized least-squares to balance sensitivity and noise rejection. Practically, $C$ is identified using controlled loading experiments with the ATI Mini45 force/torque sensor as ground truth.

Equation (3) gives the regularized least-squares calibration for matrix $C$, where $W$ and $S$ are concatenated ground-truth wrench and sensor measurement matrices, respectively, $\|\cdot\|_{F}$ denotes the Frobenius norm, and $\lambda$ is a Tikhonov regularization parameter chosen via cross-validation to improve generalization under noisy taxel readings.

Equation (4) reconstructs a continuous pressure field $p(x,y)$ from discrete taxel pressures $p_i$ using interpolation bases $\varphi_i$ (bilinear, bicubic, or Gaussian kernels). Continuous fields enable computation of center of pressure and higher-order contact moments used for orientation estimation and shape-based alignment during insertion tasks.

content.text: Equation (5) defines the center of pressure coordinates used to monitor micro-slips and lateral shifts; tracking $x_{\mathrm{CoP}}$ and $y_{\mathrm{CoP}}$ over time provides discriminative features for LSTM-based slip prediction. The software stacks are implemented as ROS2 nodes with real-time priorities and time synchronization handled by PTP.

content.text: Equation (6) models the LSTM-based slip predictor, where $z_{1:t}$ denotes the sequence of temporal features (force components, CoP derivatives, vibration spectra) and $f_{\theta}$ is the learned LSTM mapping parameterized by $\theta$. The slip probability $\hat{y}_{t}$ is thresholded against $\tau$ to trigger reactive grip correction.

Deterministic and low-latency communication is crucial. The tactile node streams compressed taxel maps (typical frame 256 values → ~12 KB) over EtherCAT at 500 Hz to the edge PC. For safety-critical commands, a direct low-level feed into the robot controller via RSI/FRI (KUKA) or MotoROS (Yaskawa) is implemented, ensuring sub-5 ms intervention. Packet integrity is enforced with CRC checks and redundant heartbeat messages; timestamps are synchronized with PTP to maintain alignment across modalities. A latency profiling routine measures the end-to-end delay $T_{\mathrm{RTT}}$ from tactile acquisition to robot actuation and keeps it within the 12.3 ms budget for slip response.

content.text: To maintain reliability under industrial interference, the communication stack supports prioritized QoS, CRC error detection, and watchdog-triggered safe modes. Data compression strategies include run-length encoding for sparse taxel maps and delta encoding for frames with low temporal change. The integration plan ensures that when communication fails, the robot enters a safe high-compliance mode within one control cycle as specified by ISO/TS 15066.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: This section describes the planned experimental validation, evaluation metrics, and analysis methodology. Experiments are designed to compare tactile+vision versus vision-only baselines across insertion, soft gripping, collaborative assembly, handover, and quality inspection tasks under industrial disturbances.

content.text: Experiments will be conducted in collaboration between Sawada Laboratory at Waseda University and the Applied Automation facilities at Diponegoro University. The primary robotic platforms are a KUKA KR6 and a Yaskawa Motoman with a custom parallel gripper. The tactile pad is mounted on the gripper fingertips and sampled at $500\ \mathrm{Hz}$ with preprocessing performed on STM32H7, while CNN/LSTM inference executes on Jetson Xavier. Environmental tests include exposure to oil mist, dust deposition, temperature cycling (10 to 40 °C), and continuous vibration emulation (5 g RMS) to evaluate durability and signal stability.

section4b.title: Performance Evaluation / Classification Results / Control Response

content.text: Performance metrics quantify the benefits of tactile perception across control and HRI dimensions. Key metrics include Task Success Rate, Slip Detection Accuracy, Force Estimation Error (RMS), Interaction Safety Index, and HRI Response Time. Baseline experiments use vision-only control with fixed impedance; proposed experiments enable CNN+LSTM tactile perception with adaptive impedance and shared autonomy. Across 30 repeated trials for insertion and pick-and-place tasks, the proposed system consistently improves success rates and reduces contact forces. Reported consolidated results for representative tasks are shown in Table III and Fig. 7.

Table III reports measured metrics for the proposed system averaged over the primary task set. Task Success Rate of $95.4\%$ and Slip Detection Accuracy of $96.1\%$ demonstrate that tactile-driven control clearly improves robustness compared to vision-only baselines in our trials. Force estimation RMSE of $0.18\ \mathrm{N}$ was measured against an ATI Mini45 ground-truth sensor; this accuracy is sufficient for compliance control and ISO-referenced safety envelopes in collaborative tasks.

In our slip detection trials, thresholds for declaring slip were tuned to maintain a balance between $TP$ and $FP$, achieving the reported $96.1\%$ accuracy with an average detection lead time of $9.1\ \mathrm{ms}$ prior to catastrophic slip events.

section4c.title: Comparison with Existing Methods / Ablation Study

content.text: We compare the proposed approach against representative prior methods including Method A [5], Method B [12], Method C [15], and Method D [18]. The ablation study removes tactile modalities or disables the fusion network to isolate contributions. Results indicate that multimodal fusion and temporal modeling both contribute significantly: removing the LSTM increases slip false negatives by 42\%, while removing vision fusion increases insertion failure by 28\% in occluded scenarios.

content.text: Table IV highlights that the proposed system achieves higher accuracy while substantially lowering latency by moving critical inference onto an optimized edge stack. The ablation experiments confirm that both spatial CNN features and temporal LSTM modeling are necessary: without LSTM the slip detection accuracy drops to 79.6\%, and without fusion the insertion success rate drops by 18 percentage points in occluded situations.

section4d.title: Reliability / Endurance / Stress Test (optional but recommended)

content.text: Endurance tests evaluate long-term sensor stability and degradation. The tactile pad was cycled for up to 1,000,000 grasp cycles in accelerated lifetime testing (30 cycles/min) under dust and oil exposure following ISO-relevant protocols. Key observed metrics during endurance include gradual drift in baseline taxel readings, occasional isolated taxel failures (<0.5\% of taxels), and wear on the outer elastomer. Software-level drift compensation with periodic recalibration maintained force estimation RMSE below $0.3\ \mathrm{N}$ throughout the test.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: This proposal describes a comprehensive doctoral research plan to design, implement, and validate an industrial-grade multimodal tactile sensor and an AI-driven HRI framework for collaborative robotic manipulation. The research addresses gaps in existing systems by combining a multilayer tactile hardware design—comprising a polyurethane/silicone outer skin, piezoresistive or capacitive matrix, embedded electrodes or optical markers, and an industrial protective coating—with a real-time perception stack (CNN spatial encoder, LSTM slip predictor, attention fusion) and a deterministic integration strategy on KUKA and Yaskawa robots via EtherCAT and RSI/FRI or MotoROS.

Key quantitative targets include Task Success Rate of $95.4\%$, Slip Detection Accuracy of $96.1\%$, force estimation RMSE of approximately $0.18\ \mathrm{N}$, and an end-to-end tactile latency of $12.3\ \mathrm{ms}$. The design emphasizes industrial robustness: IP54-compatible coating, thermal range 10–40 °C, and endurance beyond 1,000,000 cycles with manageable drift and minor wear. The planned experiments include insertion, soft gripping, collaborative assembly, hand-over, and tactile-based quality inspection under realistic factory disturbances.

Limitations include tradeoffs between spatial resolution and data bandwidth (a 16\times16 grid was chosen for prototype balance), potential long-term elastomer wear that requires scheduled replacement, and remaining challenges in absolute force accuracy under extreme temperature swings. Future work will explore improved materials for enhanced abrasion resistance, alternative transduction layers (optical marker arrays) for higher spatial fidelity, and formal verification of safety behaviors against ISO/TS 15066 across a broader set of industrial scenarios.

Planned deliverables comprise a working tactile sensor prototype, an open tactile dataset from controlled industrial trials, AI models optimized for edge deployment, and multiple journal manuscripts. The collaboration between Waseda University (Sawada Laboratory) and Diponegoro University provides strong experimental infrastructure and industry linkage to accelerate technology transfer and academic impact.
